claims.text: Residual in-plane strain and surface/interface defects primarily govern the low-field magnetocaloric response and hysteresis of as-deposited FeMnNiGeSi-type thin films and nanoribbons.
Residual strain and interface defects pin the martensitic transformation.
As-deposited FeMnNiGeSi-type nanoscale films and nanoribbons exhibit significant residual strain and defect density.
The controlled intervention is rapid thermal annealing at approximately 500 °C for 60 seconds in an inert atmosphere.
The proposed RTA treatment will partially relieve internal strain and reduce defect concentrations without altering nanoscale morphology.
Reducing residual strain and defect density will moderate spatial inhomogeneity in the martensitic transformation.
Improved transformation uniformity will make the phase change more reversible by easing domain-wall motion and reducing pinning forces.
Residual strain and interface defects create energy barriers that hinder phase transformation, broaden the transition, and increase thermal hysteresis.
RTA-induced strain relaxation and defect removal will decrease pinning of phase-boundary motion.
Decreased phase-boundary pinning will produce a sharper, more coherent transformation with reduced hysteresis.
RTA-treated samples will exhibit less thermal hysteresis than the as-deposited baseline.
RTA-treated samples will exhibit a sharper magnetocaloric peak than the as-deposited baseline.
Improved transformation reversibility after RTA will support higher magnetic-cooling cycle frequencies.
RTA may modestly reduce the peak magnetic entropy change by decreasing the phase-coexistence window.
The proposed mechanism applies to 10–50 nm films or similarly scaled nanoribbons under fields below 0.5 T and temperatures near 300–350 K.
The mechanism may cease to apply at substantially larger dimensions or when annealing causes excessive grain growth or phase decomposition.
Heat-transfer rate limits the attainable cycle frequency in the specified nanoscale regime.
